desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

Swap every two adjacent nodes of the list: the 1st and 2nd node trade places, then the 3rd and 4th, and so on. If the length is odd, the last node stays where it is. Return the values of the resulting list from head to tail.

For example [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [2,1,4,3,5]. In a real list you must exchange the nodes by relinking pointers, not just copy values between them.
hints: Look at one pair a -> b that is preceded by some node prev. After the swap you need prev -> b -> a -> (whatever followed b).
A dummy node placed before the head means the first pair is handled exactly like every other pair, and you never special-case the new head.

Loop while prev.next and prev.next.next both exist: take a = prev.next, b = a.next; set a.next = b.next, b.next = a, prev.next = b; then move prev to a, which is now the second node of the swapped pair.
editorial: Place a dummy node in front of the head and keep a prev pointer to the node just before the current pair. For a pair a, b three pointers change: a.next skips over b, b.next points back to a, and prev.next points to b. After that a is the last node of the finished pair, so it becomes the new prev. The loop stops when fewer than two nodes remain, which automatically leaves a lone last node untouched.
Each node is visited once, so the time is O(n) and only a constant number of pointers is used. A recursive solution (swap the first two, recurse on the rest) is shorter but uses O(n) stack.
